messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
Carlos had been driving home late after a gig, still carrying the last echoes of the set in his head, when a life-threatening accident changed the shape of everything that came after. He remembered the sudden violence of it in pieces rather than as a single story: the impact, the crush of metal, the jolt that threw his body forward, the sound of something breaking, then moments that seemed to vanish before returning in another fragment. In the days that followed, when others asked him what had happened, he found he could not deliberately bring the memory into view in a coherent way. He knew he had been there, knew the danger had been real, but when he tried to recount it, the details slipped apart and left him with a scattered impression that felt unfinished, as though the central part of the event were still missing. What remained were disconnected flashes that did not fit together into the full picture he felt should be there.

In the weeks after the accident, Carlos began to structure his life around staying in motion and staying with people. As a married man who worked as a musician, he had once been comfortable with long stretches of solitude while writing, rehearsing, or driving between venues, but now he kept himself constantly surrounded by others so that he would not be left alone with his thoughts. He arranged to be with bandmates, friends, or family whenever possible, lingering after rehearsals and making himself available for late dinners, not because he particularly wanted company every moment, but because silence made the accident feel closer. He found that being alone gave him too much room to drift toward the event and toward the parts of it he could not fully retrieve. He also became careful about what he talked about. When people brought up the crash, the hospital, or how he had been doing since, Carlos would steer the conversation elsewhere, offer a joke, ask about their lives, or simply let the topic die. He did not want to go over the event or what followed it, partly because he felt he could not tell it properly and partly because he did not want the details to gather force in the room.

As time passed, the accident became something he worked hard not to think about directly. That effort showed up in ordinary moments: while waiting backstage before a performance, during a quiet morning at home, or on a drive through the city, he would catch himself approaching the subject in his mind and then force attention elsewhere. His wife noticed that he became more eager to fill evenings with plans, and his bandmates came to expect that Carlos would be the one suggesting another round after a set, another gathering after rehearsal, anything that kept the night from settling into stillness. He had come to believe that what happened to him was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it. The sense of injustice stayed with him, especially when he thought of the ordinary fact that he had left for work and nearly not made it home at all. He felt that the accident had stolen something from him that should never have been taken, and that no amount of explanation or sympathy could put that right.

What frightened Carlos most was the anger he felt flickering beneath the surface. He was certain that if he let himself dwell too long on what had happened, he would not be able to control his rage and might do something terrible. He did not always know exactly who that rage was aimed at, only that it felt dangerous to him, the kind of feeling that could expand beyond words. For that reason, he avoided conversations that might open the door to it and kept himself busy with other people, where he could monitor his reactions and stay outwardly composed. Yet even with all the movement and company, there were moments when the whole event seemed to press against him from the edges of memory, leaving him with the sense that his life had been altered in a way he could not undo. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, not in a dramatic instant but in the quieter, accumulating way that followed: the need to keep himself surrounded, the refusal to talk, the effort not to think, and the persistent feeling that the version of his life before the accident was gone.

By the time Carlos sought help, he was worn down by maintaining this pattern and by the strain it placed on his marriage and work. Being a musician meant his life was already built around performance, connection, and long nights in crowded spaces, yet now even those familiar settings had become part refuge and part burden, because they let him stay distracted while also reminding him how different he felt from the person who used to move through them freely. He came to treatment hoping for some way to face the event without being overwhelmed by the missing pieces, the anger, and the conviction that everything had been irreparably ruined. More than anything, he wanted to know whether he could stop living as if he were always one step away from the accident returning, and whether there was any chance of recovering a life that still felt his own.
